extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students and interested general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Expository treatment of the real number continuum, definitions of irrational numbers (via infinite decimals, nested intervals, Dedekind cuts, and Cauchy sequences), basic analytic geometry, and Cantorian set-theoretic results about countability and cardinality. Aimed to present multiple equivalent constructions and philosophical remarks on foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition via infinite decimals
rubrics_metrics.description: The continuum of numbers (real number system) is the totality of infinite decimals. The rational numbers are the periodic decimals; the irrational numbers are the non-periodic decimals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finite decimals may be regarded as infinite decimals with trailing zeros or as an alternative representation with trailing 9's (.999... = 1). This decimal-based definition is convenient but not singled out by nature: equivalent constructions exist in other bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition via nested intervals (axiom/postulate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any sequence of nested intervals on the number axis with rational endpoints, each contained in the previous one, whose lengths tend to zero, corresponds to precisely one point on the number axis; that point is called a real number (irrational if not rational).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a basic postulate of geometry; uniqueness follows because lengths tend to zero. The construction frees the definition from dependence on base-ten decimals and gives an 'intrinsic' definition of real numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrational point as symbol for nested rational intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: Formally an irrational point may be treated as a symbol denoting a sequence of nested rational intervals with lengths tending to zero; all properties of such points are expressed as properties of those sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical justification: mathematical objects are defined by their properties and relations rather than as 'things in themselves'; this intrinsic viewpoint replaces naive realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of arithmetic operations to reals
rubrics_metrics.description: Addition, multiplication, subtraction, division and order relations for real (including irrational) numbers must be defined in terms of the underlying constructions (e.g., nested intervals) so that the arithmetical laws holding for rationals are preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: add two reals defined by nested-interval sequences by adding corresponding left and right endpoints to form a new nested-interval sequence; similar constructions define product, difference and quotient. Verification is straightforward though sometimes tedious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical/physical interpretation requiring continuum
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational numbers correspond to limits of sequences of ever-more-precise measurements; although any finite measurement cannot determine rationality, the continuum simplifies mathematical descriptions (via limits) of physical phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivates the utility of introducing irrational numbers for calculus and limit concepts despite their physical indistinguishability from rationals in finite measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedekind cut definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A cut divides rationals into two classes A and B such that every element of B is greater than every element of A. If neither A has a largest element nor B a smallest element, the cut defines an irrational number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three possible cases are enumerated (largest in A, smallest in B, or neither). This abstract approach is equivalent to nested intervals; it emphasizes an abstract classification of rationals into two complementary sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor (Cauchy sequence) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Any sequence of rational numbers that 'converges' (difference between far-out terms tends to zero) defines a real number; two convergent sequences define the same real if their termwise difference tends to zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This abstracts from decimal expansions: infinite decimals are limits of finite decimal fractions. Operations on reals are defined on equivalence classes of convergent rational sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinates characterize geometric objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigning coordinates (numbers) to geometric objects (points) completely characterizes those objects; rectangular (Cartesian) coordinates assign two numbers to each plane point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinates arise from choosing two perpendicular directed axes measured with the same unit; conversely, any pair of numbers determines a unique point. Quadrant classification depends on sign of coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclidean distance formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Distance between points (x1,y1) and (x2,y2) is d = sqrt((x1 - x2)^2 + (y1 - y2)^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows directly from the Pythagorean theorem and serves as the metric when translating geometry into algebraic terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equations as necessary and sufficient locus conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: An algebraic equation in coordinates expresses the necessary and sufficient condition for a point to belong to a geometric locus (e.g., (x-a)^2 + (y-b)^2 = r^2 is the equation of a circle centered at (a,b) with radius r).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversely, given an algebraic equation of appropriate form and constants satisfying constraints (e.g., positivity), one can identify the geometric locus it represents via algebraic manipulation such as completing the square.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical linear equation for lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Any straight line has an equation of the form ax + by = c where a, b, c are fixed constants characterizing the line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special cases correspond to coordinate axes (y=0, x=0) and bisectors (x=y, x=-y).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conic classification and properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard algebraic equations classify conics: ellipse (x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 =1), hyperbola, equilateral hyperbola (xy = c), with associated geometric notions like major/minor axes, foci and eccentricity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric properties (intercepts, foci, asymptotes) are derivable from the algebraic form; e.g., ellipse locus characterized by sum of distances to foci equals constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection by solving simultaneous equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Points of intersection of curves/lines are found by solving their corresponding simultaneous algebraic equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard analytic-geometry method: convert geometric intersection problems to algebraic equation systems and solve for coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'infinite' from 'infinity' (do not treat infinity as a number)
rubrics_metrics.description: The adjective 'infinite' (without end) differs from the noun 'infinity'; the symbol ∞ cannot be included as an ordinary number in the real number system without violating arithmetic rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infinity is a conceptual notion used in analysis of sets and limits but must not be conflated with real numbers when preserving arithmetic laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set equivalence via biunique correspondence (cardinality principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sets are equivalent (have the same cardinal number) if there exists a biunique (bijective) correspondence between their elements. This extends the notion of 'same number of elements' to infinite sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational notion used to compare sizes of finite and infinite sets: equivalence reduces to ordinary equality for finite sets, but behaves counterintuitively for infinite ones (e.g., integers vs even integers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Denumerability and a constructive denumeration of rationals
rubrics_metrics.description: A set is denumerable if its elements can be arranged in a sequence like the integers; the rational numbers are denumerable via an explicit array and a diagonal traversal with cancellation of reducible fractions so each rational appears once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook gives a concrete traversal scheme (zig-zag/diagonal) through an array a/b (columns/rows), then cancels fractions with common factors to obtain a sequence listing every positive rational exactly once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor diagonal argument for non-denumerability of reals
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a sequence listing all real numbers as infinite decimals; construct a new decimal by choosing its nth digit different from the nth digit of the nth number (avoiding 0 and 9 to prevent 0.999... ambiguity). The constructed number differs from every listed number, so the reals are not denumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit advice: choose digits for the diagonal number that are neither 0 nor 9 to avoid equality ambiguities like 0.999... = 1.000.... This is the canonical diagonalization method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of intervals and whole line (cardinality invariance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any finite segment of the number axis is equivalent (has same cardinal number) to the whole real line; there exist explicit bijections (e.g., via bending and projection) between segments and lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, non-denumerability is a property even of finite intervals like (0,1). Exercises include showing any interval [A,B] is equivalent to any other [C,D].

rubrics_metrics.name: Denumerable sets have measure zero (measure-theoretic observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any denumerable set of points on the line can be covered by intervals of arbitrarily small total length (hence countable sets have measure zero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: enclose nth point in an interval of length c/10^n; the sum is c/9, and since c is arbitrary, total length can be made arbitrarily small. Similar result holds in the plane replacing lengths with areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power set increases cardinality (Cantor's theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any set A there exists a set (the set of all subsets of A, the power set) whose cardinal number is strictly greater than that of A; equivalently, no bijection exists between A and its power set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof method: assume bijection between elements a of A and subsets S_a of A, then construct a subset T = {x in A | x not in S_x} and derive contradiction by showing T has no preimage under the bijection (diagonal-like argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive vs non-constructive existence proofs (methodological criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an essential difference between demonstrating existence by explicit construction (tangible example) and proving existence indirectly by contradiction; some schools (intuitionism) favor constructive proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-constructive proofs can be simpler or more powerful, and banning them would cause major complications and loss in mathematics. The text notes philosophical debates and practical resistance to pure constructivism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of paradoxes of the infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinite sets lead to counterintuitive phenomena (e.g., a set equivalent to a proper subset), and these paradoxes necessitate careful definitions and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats several paradoxical outcomes (integers vs even integers; rationals vs integers) as motivations for rigorous set-theoretic treatment and further development (Cantor's cardinal numbers).
